text:
A mutex keeps threads in a program from stepping on each other. It guards a critical section, the part of the code that touches shared data, and only one thread can hold it at a time. Any other thread that wants in has to wait until the lock is released. It works a bit like a bouncer at a busy club: one person goes in and everyone else waits in line.

Mutexes are easy to misuse. If threads grab locks in the wrong order, you can end up with a deadlock, where each thread waits on another and none of them ever moves.

On Linux, mutexes are built on futexes. When no other thread holds the lock, a thread can take it without making a system call, so the common uncontended case stays fast.

You'll keep running into mutexes whether you're writing a game or a banking app, so they're worth learning well.
